fr:title.text: A type theory for geometric theories

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: A type theory for geometric theories

fr:mainmatter.html:p: (This is meant for The categorical logician)

The ultimate intended semantics for Coln is in arithmetic theories, which are the analogue of geometric theories for arithmetic universes. However, geometric theories and topoi are both better-studied than arithmetic universes and are additionally closely related, so we give an exposition of the basic type theory in terms of geometric theories. Note that by topos we mean Grothendieck topos, not elementary topos, so in particular all topoi have natural numbers objects.

Following the principles of this manual, this is not a mathematical paper; there will be a more formal account of this type theory, but that is in progress. Rather, this is a conceptual account that makes reference to mathematics.
In The Elephant, Johnstone makes the following definitions for “theory”; we call this an elephant theory in order to distinguish it from other notions of theory we might consider.

For \mathcal {S} a topos, an elephant theory over \mathcal {S} is a (pseudo-)functor T \colon (\mathsf {BTop}/\mathcal {S})^\mathrm {op} \to \mathsf {Cat}, where (\mathsf {BTop}/\mathcal {S})^\mathrm {op} is the 2-category of bounded geometric morphisms into \mathcal {S} and \mathsf {Cat} is the 2-category of large categories.
A morphism of elephant theories is simply an indexed functor.

We say that T is classified by \mathsf {S}[T] \colon \mathsf {BTop}/\mathcal {S} if T is contravariantly represented by \mathcal {S}[T], that is T(\mathcal {E}) \cong \mathsf {BTop}/\mathcal {S}(\mathcal {E}, \mathcal {S}[T]). We also call \mathsf {S}[T] the classifying topos for T.
(See Elephant Definition B4.2.1)

The object classifier \mathbb {O} is the elephant theory defined by the forgetful functor (\mathsf {BTop}/\mathcal {S})^\mathrm {op} \to \mathsf {Cat} which sends a bounded topos over \mathcal {S} to its underlying category of objects.
(See Elephant Example B4.2.4(a))
If T is a geometric theory, then a geometric construct is a \mathsf {BTop}/\mathcal {S}-indexed functor F \colon T \to \mathbb {O}.
The idea is that F, given a model M of T in an \mathcal {S}-topos \mathcal {E}, produces an object of \mathcal {E}.
(See Elephant Definition B4.2.5)
Geometric theories may be consicely defined as the elephant theories built up via a sequence of product-inserter-equifier limits starting from the object classifier.
We expand this to give more intuition.

If T is a theory, a simple functional extension of T is another theory T' given as the inserter of two geometric constructs F,G \colon T \to \mathbb {O}. Intuitively, T' is the theory given by freely adding a new morphism between the “objects” F and G.

If T is a theory, a simple equational extension of T is another theory T' given as the equifier of two indexed natural transformations \alpha , \beta \colon F \Rightarrow G, where F and G are geometric constructs. Intuitively, T' is the theory given by adding a new equality between morphisms of “objects”.
A geometric theory is a theory built up by a finite sequence T_0,\ldots ,T_n of simple functional extensions and simple equational extensions starting from T_0 = \mathbb {O}^m for some finite m.

(See Elephant Definition 4.2.7, note that Johnstone gives a slightly different definition, using simple geometric quotients in place of simple equational extensions, which use inverters instead of equifiers. The name “simple equational extension” is not known to us to be previously used, but it follows the schema of “simple functional extension.”)
Any geometric theory has a classifying topos.
(See Elephant Theorem 4.2.9)

fr:title.text: A category with families structure on elephant theories

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: A category with families structure on elephant theories

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Let \mathsf {ElTh} be the category of elephant theories. Then let \mathsf {Ty} \colon \mathsf {ElTh}^\mathrm {op} \to \mathsf {SET} be the large presheaf which sends an elephant theory \Gamma to the set of strict 2-functors A \colon (\int \Gamma )^\mathrm {op} \to \mathsf {Cat}.

Intuitively, \mathsf {Ty}(\Gamma ) is “elephant theories relative to \Gamma .” This is because \int \Gamma is the category of topoi equipped with a model of \Gamma ; if \Gamma were a geometric theory then \int \Gamma would be equivalent to \mathsf {BTop}/\mathcal {S}[\Gamma ].

Then define \mathsf {Tm} \colon (\int \mathsf {Ty})^\mathrm {op} \to \mathsf {Set} by letting \mathsf {Tm}(\Gamma , A) be the set of sections of A. A section a is a natural assignment of a(\mathcal {E}, M) \colon A(\mathcal {E}, M) for (\mathcal {E},M) \in \int \Gamma .

Context extension is given in the following way. Suppose that \Gamma \colon (\mathsf {BTop}/\mathcal {S})^\mathrm {op} \to \mathsf {Cat} is a context and A \colon \mathsf {Ty}(\Gamma ). Then \Gamma \triangleright A \colon (\mathsf {BTop}/\mathcal {S})^\mathrm {op} \to \mathsf {Cat} is defined by (\Gamma \triangleright A)(\mathcal {E}) = (M \colon \Gamma (\mathcal {E})) \times A(\mathcal {E},M).
Then finally we have weakening and the variable rule given by the first and second projections out of \Gamma \triangleright A.
Note that even though topoi and elephant theories are non-trivially 2-categorical, (\mathsf {ElTh},\mathsf {Ty},\mathsf {Tm}) forms nevertheless a strict (albeit quite large) category with families.
The remainder of this section is simply an investigation of what type formers are supported in \mathsf {ElTh}.

fr:title.text: Type theory as a language for anything

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Type theory as a language for anything

fr:mainmatter.html:p: (This is meant for The type theorist, The database engineer, The developer, The programmer-user)

A programmer with a passing familiarity with type theory may have formed some preconceptions about what a type is, and what it means to give an element of that type. For instance, in a language like Haskell or Rust, types are how we put structure on pieces of computer memory, so that we remember that the value at a certain address is a pointer or integer or floating point number. In a proof assistant, types are used as a foundation for mathematics; types play the role of the “sets” that informal mathematicians use.

The truth is that types do not have any intrinsic meaning. Rather, type theory is a convenient tool for working with any collection of things which relate to each other in certain precise, well-structured ways.
In particular, type theory is a tool for working with things defined by universal properties.
In set theory, if A and B are sets then to produce an element of A \times B it suffices to produce an element of A and an element of B, and vice-versa.
In propositional logic, if P and Q are propositions then to produce a proof of P \wedge Q it suffices to produce a proof of P and a proof of Q, and vice-versa.
In a programming language with tuple types, if a and b are types then to produce an element of (a,b) it suffices to produce an element of a and an element of b, and vice-versa.
In number theory, in order to show that k is a divisor of the GCD (greatest common divisor) of m and n, it suffices show that k is a divisor of m and n, and vice versa.
Again in set theory, if U and V are subsets of a larger set X, then to show that x is an element of U \cap V it suffices to show that x is an element of U and an element of V, and vice-versa.
In group theory, in order to produce a homomorphism from G to the product group H_0 \times H_1, it suffices to produce a homomorphism from G to H_0 and from G to H_1, and vice-versa.
This list could consider ad nauseum, but the reader should get the point by now; there's a pattern going on.
The concept of a universal property is formalized in different ways, often using category theory, but we need not bother with formalization at this stage.

The reader may have heard of “the Curry-Howard correspondence”, often informally referred to “propositions as types”. The Curry-Howard correspondence shows how various type formers and logical connectives correspond. With all due respect to Curry-Howard the name “correspondence” is somewhat of a misnomer because it assumes a false equivalence between the two things that are claimed to be in correspondence. In particular, propositional logic is a mathematical domain in which type theory may be applied to form a convenient syntax; it is by no means the only domain.

The reason type theory may be usefully applied to propositional logic because all of the connectives of propositional logic (and, or, not, forall, exists, etc.) satisfy universal properties; this is the same as the reason why type theory may be applied to any other area.

The way that type theory may be applied to a particular area is via the development of a particular type theory. Confusion between type theory as a subject and the concept of a type theory as a mathematical object is an unfortunate side effect of the nomenclature, because “ breaks with the convention that in group theory, we study groups, in field theory we study fields, or in category theory we study categories.

A particular type theory is merely a syntactic formalization of some collection of universal properties, consisting of a collection of rules by which we judge that a certain piece of syntax is well-typed. The beauty of universal properties is that each universal property is quite self-contained, so a type theory may be designed by systematically observing which universal properties the objects of interest support, and then adding the standard type-theoretic rules for those universal properties to one's type theory.

And this is the method that we have followed in order to design the type theory for Coln: observe the universal properties that our domain of interest (relational databases) satisfy, and add rules corresponding to these universal properties. Fortunately, the result of this systematic development seems to produce a language which expresses many of the important database operations.
